tokens: You fixed it by making every transaction take its row locks in the same order.
The deadlock came from two workers upserting the same rows in different orders [Memory 1].
You sorted each batch by primary key before the `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`,
cut the batch size from 5000 to 500,
and added a retry on SQLSTATE `40P01` with jitter, three attempts at most [Memory 2].
Your notes on the book chapter explain why the retry is still needed:
the database breaks a lock cycle by aborting one transaction,
and the application has to run it again [Memory 3].

sources.excerpt:
[ASSISTANT]
The deadlock comes from two transactions upserting the same set of rows in a different order\. Each takes a row lock the other needs. Sort the batch by primary key before the INSERT ... ON CONFLICT so every transaction acquires its locks in the same order.

[USER]
Sorting fixed it in staging. I also dropped the batch size from 5000 to 500 and added a retry on SQLSTATE 40P01 with jitter, three attempts max. My pick\: keep the retry even if the sort holds up.

Deadlocks arise when transactions wait on each other in a cycle. The database detects the cycle and aborts one of them so that the others can make progress; the aborted transaction must be retried by the application.

[CLAUDE]
For the migration, take an advisory lock first so only one worker runs it. pg_advisory_xact_lock releases at commit, which is what you want here.
Order the Dockerfile so dependency installation comes before copying the source. The lockfile changes rarely, so that layer stays cached.
